question: Why does a brioche dough rich in sugar rise more slowly than a plain one made with the same yeast?
answer: Sugar pulls water out of the yeast. A concentrated sugar solution draws water across the cell's membrane, so the cells shrink and slow down. Above roughly 10% sugar on the flour's weight, ordinary baker's yeast struggles. Suppliers sell osmotolerant strains for sweet doughs: cells that pile up glycerol inside to hold on to their water.
move: Past a point, more of the food can starve the eater of something else.
reference: Cauvain & Young, Baked Products: Science, Technology and Practice, Blackwell Publishing, 2006
